article_title: Learning with multiple representations: An example of a revision lesson in mechanics
citation: Darren Wong, Sng Peng Poo, Ng Eng Hock and Wee Loo Kang. (2010). Learning with multiple representations: an example of a revision lesson in mechanics. Submitted to IOP Publishing for peer review. http://www.phy.ntnu.edu.tw/ntnujava/index.php?topic=1940.0
title: An Easy Java Simulations program that dynamically plots graphs alongside a diagrammatic view of the ball's motion
description: The authors "created a simulation using Easy Java Simulations (Ejs)" to support active learning with multiple representations in the mechanics lesson. The program "dynamically plot[s] out the shapes of different graphs with the diagrammatic view of the motion of the ball", including energy bar charts before energy graphs, and can draw the ball's trace "akin to the motion diagram discussed earlier". It is offered for extension activities such as multi-bounce motion and comparing graphs with and without air resistance.
requirements: Only selected variables are visible at a time so that the simulation "focuses learning without unnecessary cognitive overloading"
constraints: It is offered as a computer-supported complement to, not a replacement for, the classroom lesson with multiple representations
target_learners: A-level (junior college) physics students in Singapore
target_learning_goals: Relating displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum and energy representations of vertical ball motion
examples: Students can be guided to predict what graphs with air resistance might look like and check against those obtained from the simulation
Exploring the ball's motion for more than one bounce and at different conditions of elasticity of impact with the ground
key_sources: Darren Wong, Sng Peng Poo, Ng Eng Hock and Wee Loo Kang. (2010). Learning with multiple representations: an example of a revision lesson in mechanics. Submitted to IOP Publishing for peer review. http://www.phy.ntnu.edu.tw/ntnujava/index.php?topic=1940.0

article_title: Leveraging on Easy Java Simulation tool and open source computer simulation library to create interactive digital media for mass customization of high school physics curriculum
citation: Loo Kang Wee & Wai Keong Mak. (2009). Leveraging on Easy Java Simulation tool and open source computer simulation library to create interactive digital media for mass customization of high school physics curriculum. Paper presented at the 3rd Redesigning Pedagogy International Conference, Singapore. http://conference.nie.edu.sg/2009/
title: One-dimensional collision virtual laboratory for A-level physics (linear momentum and its conservation)
description: The authors remixed the community-supplied Collision1D.xml expert source file into an educator-customized "interactive digital media and virtual laboratory" for the difficult A-level topics of linear momentum and kinetic energy conservation in elastic and inelastic collisions. The design includes collision-cart visuals with wheels, adjustable velocity arrows positioned above the carts to match textbook mental representations, Boolean-controlled dynamic hints displaying the momentum conservation equation, radio buttons selecting elastic (e = 1.0) or inelastic (e = 0.0) states, and dynamic graph plotting of momentum. It is released freely online as a downloadable jar file, Ejs XML source, and worksheets.
requirements: Ejs installation with the workspace source file Collision1D.xml
Radio-button logic restricting the collision type to one legal state at a time
target_learners: A-level physics students
target_learning_goals: linear momentum and its conservation
kinetic energy conservation in perfectly elastic and inelastic collisions
inquiry learning through a manipulative virtual laboratory
key_sources: Loo Kang Wee & Wai Keong Mak. (2009). Leveraging on Easy Java Simulation tool and open source computer simulation library to create interactive digital media for mass customization of high school physics curriculum. Paper presented at the 3rd Redesigning Pedagogy International Conference, Singapore. http://conference.nie.edu.sg/2009/

article_title: Leveraging on Easy Java Simulation tool and open source computer simulation library to create interactive digital media for mass customization of high school physics curriculum
citation: Loo Kang Wee & Wai Keong Mak. (2009). Leveraging on Easy Java Simulation tool and open source computer simulation library to create interactive digital media for mass customization of high school physics curriculum. Paper presented at the 3rd Redesigning Pedagogy International Conference, Singapore. http://conference.nie.edu.sg/2009/
title: Virtual laboratory design pattern for inquiry: integer-snapped sliders, on-demand hints, and dynamic plotting
description: The paper enumerates design characteristics a simulation needs to function as an inquiry learning environment: sliders for variables with enough variation of values to let patterns and trends emerge; "The slider values can be selected to snap to closest, for ease of values selection 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 kg for example instead of 1.354 kg type of values"; sliders that reinitialize stored values; Boolean-controlled pedagogical hints appearing only when switched on; and a plotting panel with connected traces drawn in the variable's assigned color. Together these features make the simulation a manipulative tool for sense-making.
requirements: Slider variables assigned back to calculation variables in the initialization page so stored values are remembered
Boolean enable variables and a run-on-drag initialize function wired to each slider
constraints: The trace must be configured with connected = false to make plots look like real data loggers, an explicit choice the authors document
target_learners: A-level physics students
target_learning_goals: pattern recognition and trends in momentum and kinetic energy
sense-making through dynamic visual feedback
examples: mass sliders snapped to integer values 1 through 7 kg with 7 ticks, and a momentum plot with X = t, Y = mom1, connected lines and ellipse markers
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: Physics Educators as Designers of Simulation using Easy Java Simulation (Ejs) Part 2*
citation: Loo Kang WEE. (2012). Physics Educators as Designers of Simulation using Easy Java Simulation (Ejs) Part 2. American Association of Physics Teachers 2012 Winter Meeting, Ontario, California. http://www.aapt.org/Conferences/wm2012/upload/aapt-program-final2a.pdf
title: Easy Java Simulation (Ejs) open source authoring toolkit for creating physics computer simulations
description: Easy Java Simulation (Ejs) is described as "a software tool (java code generator) designed for the creation of discrete computer simulations", a free authoring toolkit the author uses to create computer models that allow students to visualize physics phenomena. Because it exposes open source codes, educators can examine "the open source codes of the simulation through the Easy Java Simulation (EJS) toolkit" and make sense of the physics from computational models created by practicing physicists. The paper positions it as the enabling tool for teacher design and remixing within the Open Source Physics community.
requirements: Access to the free Ejs toolkit and the open source digital library of simulation models from which educators examine and remix source codes
constraints: The paper describes simulation creation for physics topics; models are licensed creative commons attribution and hosted in digital libraries such as the NTNUJAVA Virtual Physics Laboratory
target_learners: Physics students, including GCE Advanced Level physics learners
target_learning_goals: Visualizing physics phenomena and conducting inquiry into wave and matter topics through computational models
examples: The author created several computer models with Ejs and customized models built on open source codes shared by the Open Source Physics community and Fu-Kwun's NTNUJAVA Virtual Physics Laboratory
key_sources: Loo Kang WEE. (2012). Physics Educators as Designers of Simulation using Easy Java Simulation (Ejs) Part 2. American Association of Physics Teachers 2012 Winter Meeting, Ontario, California. http://www.aapt.org/Conferences/wm2012/upload/aapt-program-final2a.pdf

title: Ripple Tank Model: Ejs open source two-source interference simulation with top, side and 3D views and incoherent-source option
description: An Ejs open source ripple tank interference model derived from Andrew Duffy's original work with codes from Juan Aguirregabiria's work, customized to show top and side view of the ripple tank representations commonly taught in A level Physics. The model "has 2 sources S1 and S2 and an investigative point P", adds an intensity graph on the end of the top view, includes "a check -box for incoherence sources" described as "an uncommon feature but availabl e in our model for productive inquiry into conditions of incoherence", and offers a 3D view. It is downloadable under a creative commons attribution license.
requirements: Ejs toolkit and the source models it derives from; hosting in a digital library such as the NTNUJAVA Virtual Physics Laboratory
constraints: Designed to align with the A level Physics representation of ripple tank interference and superposition of 2 point sources
target_learners: A level physics students
target_learning_goals: Inquiry into two-source interference, coherence conditions, and visualization of displacement and intensity
examples: Used as one of five teacher remixed wave simulations shared at the AAPT 2012 Winter Meeting for active inquiry learning

title: 1 & 2 Slit(s) Diffraction Model: Ejs open source Huygens-Fresel diffraction simulation with 3D visualization and inquiry variables
description: An Ejs open source double slit diffraction model derived from Fu-Kwun Hwang's original work, showing 2 slits with 5 point sources in each slit using the Huygens-Fresel principle in a 3D view. It "allows the exploration of diffraction through 1 or 2 slits using the Huygens -Fresel principle", and variables were added "to enable inquiry learning activities". The 3D visualization is described as again useful for the wave topic.

constraints: Focused on 1- or 2-slit diffraction within the conference theme of the wave nature of light and matter

title: Standing Wave in a Pipe Model: Ejs open source simulation remixed to the Singapore syllabus with v = fλ calculation inputs
description: An Ejs open source standing wave in pipes model derived from Juan Aguirregabiria's original work, showing side view and top view of the wave representation in a pipe with nodes and antinodes shown. The author remixed it "customise d to the Singapore syllabus with our teacher style of representation" and added "input fields to calculate according to the speed of sound using the formula v = f.  λ so that student can verify their numercial answers to typical pen paper problems". This links the simulation to conventional pencil-and-paper practice.

constraints: Customized specifically to the Singapore syllabus and its teacher style of representation

The author's contributions include "the forces visualization and variables that can be used for inquiry", extending the model as an inquiry environment.

article_title: Geostationary Earth Orbit Satellite Model using Easy Java Simulation
citation: Loo Kang WEE and Giam Hwee GOH. (2015). Geostationary Earth Orbit Satellite Model using Easy Java Simulation. http://iwant2study.org/ospsg/index.php/interactive-resources/physics/02-newtonian-mechanics/08-gravity/62-gravity10
title: EJS geostationary Earth orbit satellite 3D simulation model
description: A downloadable Easy Java Simulation computer model, implemented with the EJS 3D Java library, that allows students to visualize geostationary orbits near Earth and compare them with non-geostationary orbits. The authors created it to let students "visualize the phenomena" rather than only watching pre-defined videos, and customized it to the GCE Advanced Level Physics syllabus. It is released under a creative commons attribution license and downloadable from the authors' site, ComPadre Open Source Physics and the NTNUJAVA Virtual Physics Laboratory digital libraries.
requirements: Java 3D runtime; the article states the recommended system requirement for running this EJS model in Java 3D is the Intel Pentium processor.
constraints: The physics is simplified: a constant angular velocity equation rather than gravitational force modeling, which the authors note is beyond the scope of this paper.
target_learners: GCE Advanced Level physics students in junior colleges
target_learning_goals: understanding conditions for geostationary orbits: period, equatorial plane, rotation sense
examples: The model was used in junior college laboratory lessons with inquiry activities, after which qualitative surveys and informal interviews were conducted.
key_sources: Loo Kang WEE and Giam Hwee GOH. (2015). Geostationary Earth Orbit Satellite Model using Easy Java Simulation. http://iwant2study.org/ospsg/index.php/interactive-resources/physics/02-newtonian-mechanics/08-gravity/62-gravity10

article_title: Addressing learning difficulties in Newtons 1st and 3rd Laws through problem based inquiry using Easy Java Simulation
citation: Goh, K. S. A., Wee, L. K., Yip, K. W., Toh, P. Y. J., & Lye, S. Y. (2013). Addressing learning difficulties in Newton's 1st and 3rd Laws through problem based inquiry using Easy Java Simulation. NIE Redesigning Pedagogy Conference 2013. https://www.dropbox.com/s/gf1vc7qqy7l47y8/CollsionCartsAJCworksheets.zip
title: Customized Easy Java Simulation two-body collision carts virtual laboratory model
description: An Easy Java Simulation (EJS) computer model customized from Open Source Physics community code into "a virtual laboratory" showing "a world view, and a bottom control panel for student-directed inquiry activities". The physics model simulates two carts at constant velocities by ordinary differential equations and models contact impact force with a linear spring constant and coefficient of restitution, allowing students to "make sense of Newton's 1st and 3rd Laws". Released with worksheets via the printed Dropbox links.
requirements: Requires the EJS runtime/applet and the accompanying PbI problem based inquiry worksheet; teachers facilitate its use in appropriate context with challenging inquiry activities.
constraints: Its visualization value for the 3rd Law was not confirmed in the study; the authors have since improved contact-force visualization features (Figure 4) for future testing.
target_learners: Junior college physics students (GCE Advanced Level / Ordinary Level Physics, Singapore)
target_learning_goals: Newton's 1st Law (uniform motion without net force)
Newton's 3rd Law (equal and opposite contact forces during collision)
examples: Students in the experimental classes used the model within a PbI problem based inquiry lesson on Dynamics; the FGD reported students could "configure the velocity as well as the type of collision".
key_sources: Goh, K. S. A., Wee, L. K., Yip, K. W., Toh, P. Y. J., & Lye, S. Y. (2013). article_title: NRF2011-EDU001-EL001 EduLab Project Scaling-up Reflections on Using Open Source Physics
citation: Wee, Loo Kang, Lim, Ai Phing, & Lye, Sze Yee. (2014). Scaling-up Reflections on Using Open Source Physics. https://weelookang.blogspot.sg/2013/03/moe-excel-fest-2013-scaling.html
title: Easy Java Simulations (EJS) authoring toolkit and Open Source Physics models
description: Easy Java Simulations (EJS) is an authoring toolkit that, combined with Open Source Physics, lets teachers design, create and redistribute scientific-mathematical computer models. The article reports that "EJS does a great job to produce2 free (download and use), accurate and scientific models quickly that can be studied (open source codes), remixed and reused", with "no need for login or server setup", requiring only Java runtime or a modern browser. EJS 5.0, released in September 2013, generates JavaScript models viewable on mobile operating systems like Android and iOS.

constraints: Models described as requiring Java or a modern browser; no server setup needed
target_learners: Physics teachers and students in secondary and junior college settings
target_learning_goals: Interactive engagement with physics phenomena through editable computer models
examples: Models created include 1D Collision, Falling Magnet in Coil, Ripple Tank, Superposition Waves, 2 Mass Gravity, Earth-Moon Gravity, Kepler's Solar System and Geostationary Orbit

title: Ejs Open Source Alternating Current AC Generator Model Java Applet
description: An open-source Java simulation of a hand-held AC generator used in Phase 3 (Operationalizing) of the exemplar for online concept internalization of Faraday and Lenz's Laws. article_title: Understanding resonance graphs using Easy Java Simulations (EJS) and why we use EJS
citation: Loo Kang WEE, Tat Leong LEE, Charles CHEW, Darren WONG and Samuel TAN. (2015). Understanding resonance graphs using Easy Java Simulations (EJS) and why we use EJS. Phys. Educ. 50 (2015) 189-196. http://iopscience.iop.org/0031-9120/50/2/189/
title: EJS forced-resonance computer model with an array of 100 spring-mass systems across damping levels
description: A computer model created with Easy Java Simulation in which (N=100) identical spring-mass systems are subjected to "periodic driving force of equal amplitude but different driving frequencies" and different amounts of damping. It displays theoretical steady-state amplitudes as pink dots, records red maximum amplitudes, and stores data sets so different damping runs appear on one resonance graph.
requirements: Accurate tracking of maximum amplitudes requires starting data recording after "a minimum of 30 seconds or three times the value of period of free oscillation T0 divide by damping coefficient b".
constraints: For the b = 0 case the article states reaching steady state is "impossible to reach steady state amplitude regardless of time allowed to run for", so theoretical steady-state values are stored as maximum amplitudes instead.
target_learners: Singapore-Cambridge GCE Advanced Level physics students
physics educators
target_learning_goals: interpreting amplitude versus driving frequency resonance graphs
distinguishing transient from steady-state amplitude
examples: The article shows runs for no damping b=0, light damping b=0.1, critical damping b=2.0 and heavy damping b=5.0 in Figures 4-7.
key_sources: Loo Kang WEE, Tat Leong LEE, Charles CHEW, Darren WONG and Samuel TAN. (2015). Understanding resonance graphs using Easy Java Simulations (EJS) and why we use EJS. Phys. Educ. 50 (2015) 189-196. http://iopscience.iop.org/0031-9120/50/2/189/

title: Learn physics through computer modeling with EJS, with guided model editing for advanced students and inquiry use for mainstream students
description: The article recommends learning physics through computer modeling with EJS, since modeling "is an essential practice which allows students to articulate, explain and critique their ideas of the natural world". Academically inclined students progress from guided model changes to advanced models; mainstream students use ready models as interactive inquiry resources, a redefinition use the authors argue should be scaled up.
requirements: As a beginning step, students need to be guided by an EJS experienced teacher through "the steps are required to change the EJS model" before progressing to more advanced models.
target_learners: academically inclined physics students
mainstream students
target_learning_goals: learning physics through computer modeling
inquiry-based learning of forced resonance
examples: The conclusion recommends mainstream students use the resonance model as an interactive inquiry learning resource, following the how-to-use steps in section III.

article_title: Creating Electronic Books-Chapters for Computers and Tablets Using Easy Java/JavaScript Simulations, EjsS Modeling Tool
citation: Loo Kang Wee. (2020). Creating Electronic Books-Chapters for Computers and Tablets Using Easy Java/JavaScript Simulations, EjsS Modeling Tool. MPTL'20 Proceedings. http://iwant2study.org/ospsg/index.php/interactive-resources/physics/02-newtonian-mechanics/08-gravity/154-e-book-shm
title: Three-tool workflow for authoring interactive epub3 physics e-book chapters: EjsS Modeling Tool, BlueGriffon, and Mathtowebonline
description: The article documents a three-tool authoring workflow: the EjsS Modeling Tool makes interactive models and generates epub output; BlueGriffon xhtml editor creates xhtml files with texts and images with markup errors removed; Mathtowebonline generates equations in MathML format to paste into the xhtml files. The author notes EjsS "does not create the *.xhtml format texts, but rather simply packages it with the JavaScript simulations".
requirements: EjsS Modeling Tool for models and epub generation
BlueGriffon for xhtml text editing
Mathtowebonline for free MathML equations
constraints: Pictures need to size exactly to 1024x768 in dimensions for Apple iBook publication
target_learners: Educators authoring interactive physics e-books
target_learning_goals: Production of interactive open educational resources
examples: Table 1 lists the three tools and their respective purposes towards creating interactive textbook chapters
key_sources: Loo Kang Wee. (2020). Creating Electronic Books-Chapters for Computers and Tablets Using Easy Java/JavaScript Simulations, EjsS Modeling Tool. MPTL'20 Proceedings. http://iwant2study.org/ospsg/index.php/interactive-resources/physics/02-newtonian-mechanics/08-gravity/154-e-book-shm

title: EJS authoring toolkit for creating deployable HTML science simulations
description: Easy Java/JavaScript Simulations is a free modeling and authoring tool that helps instructors design, implement and deploy computer simulations of scientific and engineering processes. It follows a Model-View-Controller design pattern, letting authors specify the model (variables, equations, ODE solving) and compose the view from a palette of view elements, then generates HTML simulations that run in any browser. The article describes it as an award-winning tool whose standardized structure has enabled hundreds of educational simulations, mostly in Physics and Control Engineering.
requirements: Creating a simulation from scratch requires some training; the article notes a three-days workshop can be enough to get a good start
constraints: Pedagogically neutral: EJS neither presumes nor fosters any particular pedagogic approach
target_learners: science and engineering students using instructor-created simulations
target_learning_goals: modeling and visualization of scientific and engineering phenomena
examples: Authors select view elements from a palette to build a tree that becomes an HTML interface with buttons, sliders and animated canvases, as in the mass and spring example

title: EJS learning analytics scenario: simulations plus LMS plus Learning Record Store with a customizable _recorder
description: The article proposes an architecture in which EJS-generated simulations send real-time interaction data to an external repository: an LMS serves the simulation within a curricular unit, and a Learning Record Store (LRS) stores all user interactions together with user context such as test grades. The EJS library captures three default interaction types — mouse and touch events, actions on view elements (e.g. OnClick and OnDrag), and actions on the model (play, pause, step, reset, initialize) — detailed enough to reproduce a user session like a video player. A built-in _recorder object lets researchers fine-tune which model variables are sent and when, so features can be matched to the pedagogic research question rather than following an all-the-information-we-can-get policy.
requirements: A server must serve the simulation HTML page, and an LRS must be integrated into an LMS to store interactions and contextual user information
constraints: The full interaction record alone may be insufficient or overkill for some studies, and machine learning on every click risks overfitting and poor generalization
target_learners: students using simulations in online or unsupervised courses
target_learning_goals: understanding students' interaction strategies and learning procedures with simulations
examples: In the mass and spring example, the _recorder can be instructed to send the variables x, vx and t at every interaction, or to send a record whenever the graph reaches a maximum

title: Moodle plugin and teacher dashboard for EJS simulation learning analytics
description: The authors created a Moodle plugin that monitors and records, in real time, all standard student interactions with an EJS simulation embedded in a Moodle course. The information is displayed on an instructor dashboard with a metric of each individual student's degree of being "on task" and shows the students' current state on the simulation. The plugin is installed on the Open Source Physics at Singapore Moodle server and provides learning analytics capability for teachers running courses based on EJS simulations; it can be applied to existing simulations by regenerating them with EJS version 6.0 and installing the plugin.
requirements: Simulations must be regenerated from source code with version 6.0 of the EJS authoring toolkit and used within a Moodle course with the plugin installed
constraints: The dashboard is described as a first, basic dashboard for monitoring students' activity
target_learners: students in Moodle-based science courses; instructors supervising their participation
target_learning_goals: monitoring student participation and on-task engagement in simulation activities
examples: Figure 4 shows an EJS simulation alongside the Student Interaction Summary displayed in Moodle

title: Learning Analytics-Moodle extension (plugin) for EjsS virtual laboratories
description: A Moodle plugin developed by the authors and installed on the Open Source Physics at Singapore (OSP@SG) server that 'provides learning analytics capability for teachers running courses based on Easy JavaScript Simulation (EjsS)'. It monitors interactions with simulations such as mouse clicks, states of buttons, sliders and combo boxes, and variable assignments, and visualises learner data in real time on an instructor dashboard, including an on-task metric and current simulation state.
requirements: The simulation must be regenerated from source code with version 6.0 of the EjsS authoring toolkit, the Moodle plugin installed, and the simulation used in a Moodle course.
constraints: The functionality applies to EjsS simulations and was piloted with educational physics simulations.
target_learners: students using EjsS virtual laboratories in Moodle courses
target_learning_goals: physics learning through simulations
instructor understanding of the learning process
examples: Fig. 1 shows an EjsS simulation alongside the Student Interaction Summary displayed in Moodle.

title: Easy JavaScript Simulations (EjsS) authoring toolkit
description: EjsS is 'an authoring toolkit that provides instructors with a click-and-drag interface for generating HTML5 JavaScript simulations or virtual laboratories'. The simulations it produces are open-source, easily edited, and hosted on Open Source Physics collections at AAPT-ComPADRE and the Singapore digital library. In this work EjsS version 6.0 is the pathway through which simulations gain the learning analytics functionality of the Moodle extension.
requirements: Instructors use the toolkit's click-and-drag interface to author simulations; analytics capability requires regeneration from source with version 6.0.
constraints: The analytics functionality described in this paper is tied to version 6.0 of the EjsS authoring toolkit.
target_learners: instructors authoring physics simulations
students using the resulting HTML5 simulations
target_learning_goals: computational-physics education through open-source simulations
examples: Simulations are hosted on the AAPT-ComPADRE Open Source Physics collections and the Singapore digital library.
